House Votes to Demand Trump End Iran War or Seek Congressional Authorization
item.description:
The U.S. House of Representatives voted 220-204 on Tuesday to direct President Donald Trump to either end the ongoing military conflict with Iran or obtain explicit authorization from Congress to continue it. The bipartisan resolution, sponsored by Democratic Representative Seth Moulton of Massachusetts, marks the third time the chamber has taken this stance, reflecting growing frustration among lawmakers about the war's duration, costs, and lack of clear objectives. Seven Republicans joined Democrats in supporting the measure, which does not carry the force of law but signals increasing political pressure on the administration as midterm elections approach.
The conflict, which began with U.S. bombing campaigns in late February, has lasted far longer than the weeks-long operation initially promised by Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. item.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Argues Against AI Regulation, Advocates for Industry Self-Management
item.description: Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang recently stated at Salesforce's Dreamforce conference that AI does not require new regulations, as safety can be managed through engineering and existing legal frameworks. Huang, who has been instrumental in developing AI hardware long before the rise of ChatGPT, emphasized that AI is simply a complex computing system built by humans, making it controllable through human oversight and market forces. He argued that companies should prioritize safety by pausing development when necessary, rather than relying on new laws. Huang believes the free market will naturally drive companies to produce safe products, stating, 'If you're not confident about the safety of the products, don't release it.' He also expressed confidence in Nvidia's ambition, noting that AI's productivity boost has limitless potential for the company and industries worldwide. item.title: NYPD disability pensions under scrutiny by New York City investigators
item.description: The Department of Investigation (DOI) is examining the New York Police Department’s disability pension program to assess its cost, eligibility, and administration. The probe aims to determine whether disability pension approvals are being granted in accordance with city policies and to identify potential gaps or abuses that could impact the city’s budget. The DOI’s review comes amid broader concerns about pension costs and accountability in city government. Key focus areas include the criteria used to designate disability, the medical evaluations behind pension approvals, and whether there is sufficient oversight to prevent improper benefits. While no specific individuals or cases are named, the investigation signals heightened scrutiny of NYPD disability pensions as part of the DOI’s mandate to combat fraud and waste. The outcomes could influence future policy adjustments, eligibility standards, or enforcement actions related to police pensions.

item.title: JWST finds organized, Jupiter-like weather patterns on a nearby brown dwarf
item.description:
Astronomers have used observations from NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) to study the changing atmosphere of SIMP 0136, a brown dwarf located about 20 light-years from Earth. Brown dwarfs are objects larger and hotter than gas-giant planets but not massive enough to sustain the nuclear fusion that makes stars shine. Their atmospheres provide valuable laboratories for studying weather processes under extreme conditions.
The research team from Trinity College Dublin analyzed tiny changes in SIMP 0136’s brightness as the object rotated. They used a statistical method called principal component analysis, or PCA, to separate the most important variations in the data from smaller fluctuations and observational noise. The results showed that most of the atmospheric variability could be explained by two dominant processes: temperature changes and differences in the vertical structure of the clouds.
The researchers identified three recurring weather states rotating in and out of view.

item.title: Dating Concerns Rise as Meta Smart Glasses Become Privacy Issue on First Dates
item.description: As the use of Meta smart glasses, particularly the Ray-Bans model, becomes more prevalent in public spaces, concerns about privacy and consent during dating have intensified. The article details multiple incidents where individuals, primarily women, were covertly filmed by dates wearing Meta smart glasses without their knowledge or consent. Courtney McAnuff, a 28-year-old project manager from Toronto, recounts her experience where her date filmed her at a bar and on the subway without her permission, later posting the footage on his Instagram story. This incident, which she describes as 'super violated,' highlights the growing unease among singles about being recorded without consent. Meta sold over 7 million pairs of Ray-Bans in 2025, with the glasses increasingly infiltrating public spaces, including dating scenarios. The phenomenon has led to the nickname 'creep glasses' among users. The article also discusses broader implications, including Meta's legal challenges over privacy conc

item.title: Google Expands Gemini Notebook with Voice Conversations, Interactive Study Tools, and Short Educational Videos
item.description: Google has introduced several new AI-powered features to Gemini Notebook, enhancing its capabilities as a study and learning tool. The updates include real-time voice conversations with notebooks, interactive study overviews, expanded quiz formats, audio recording, and short educational videos. These features aim to make studying more conversational, personalized, and interactive by grounding responses in the user's own source materials. The real-time voice feature allows students to verbally ask questions about their notes and receive step-by-step explanations, interrupting or changing the conversation as needed. This turns the notebook into an interactive tutor rather than requiring typed questions. The audio recorder enables users to capture lectures and spoken thoughts directly within the app, which can be used alongside other materials for further discussion and citation. item.title: AI Swarms Emerge as Critical Defense Against Free and Ubiquitous Artificial Intelligence
item.description: The article discusses the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence, particularly focusing on the development and accessibility of frontier-level AI models. It highlights how Alibaba's Qwen3.8-27B model has enabled near-frontier AI to run on consumer devices like laptops and smartphones, making powerful AI accessible at no cost. The author argues that this shift from renting AI services to having free, local AI capabilities will transform how people interact with technology. While the article acknowledges potential benefits such as increased cognitive capacity for personal tasks, it emphasizes the significant security risks posed by the widespread availability of powerful AI. The author warns that malicious actors will now have equal access to advanced AI tools, enabling them to conduct attacks at unprecedented speed and scale. The piece suggests that the most important application of AI will be defensive - using AI to protect against other AI threats. The author notes that this def

item.title: 19th Century Photography Techniques Revealed Through 'Hidden Mother' Images
item.description: The article discusses a historical photographic practice from the 19th century where adults, often mothers, would hide beneath fabric or behind furniture to hold young children steady during long exposure times required by early cameras. These images, commonly referred to as 'hidden mother' photographs, sometimes featured men or even female assistants of the photographer. The article explains that early photography required subjects to remain perfectly still for extended periods, making it difficult to photograph infants and toddlers without assistance. The hidden figures, partially obscured by cloth or blended into the background, create a ghostly appearance that modern viewers find strange. The article emphasizes that these photographs offer valuable insight into the technical challenges and creative solutions employed in early photography. The piece is published on Vintage Everyday, a website dedicated to sharing vintage photographs and historical images. The article includes a date

item.title: Diet Changes May Reduce Biological Age Markers in Older Adults Within Four Weeks
item.description: A recent study conducted by researchers at the University of Sydney has revealed that older adults aged 65 to 75 can experience a reduction in biological age markers after just four weeks of dietary changes. The study, published in Aging Cell, examined the effects of different dietary patterns on aging-related biomarkers. Participants were randomly assigned to one of four dietary groups: omnivorous high-fat (OHF), omnivorous high-carbohydrate (OHC), semi-vegetarian high-fat (VHF), or semi-vegetarian high-carbohydrate (VHC). Each diet provided 14 percent of total energy from protein, with variations in fat and carbohydrate intake. The results showed that the omnivorous high-fat group experienced no meaningful change in biological age markers, while the other three groups demonstrated reductions in their calculated biological age. The strongest evidence was observed in the omnivorous high-carbohydrate group, which consumed a diet with 14% protein, 28-29% fat, and 53% carbohydrates. Biolo

item.title: Diesel price surge drives unexpected energy market momentum
item.description: Diesel prices and refinery dynamics have continued to push energy markets into uncharted territory, with sustained high costs and supply concerns. The piece analyzes how diesel’s persistent strength is affecting transportation costs, manufacturing margins, and broader inflation expectations. It highlights supply chain bottlenecks, seasonal demand shifts, and geopolitical tensions that compounds the commodity’s volatility. Analysts suggest that diesel’s performance is shaping policy considerations for oil markets, including inventory management, refinery utilization, and strategic petroleum reserve activity. The report also touches on how diesel trends intersect with crude pricing, refining margins, and downstream consumer prices, potentially altering near-term economic projections. item.title: Miss Manners Offers Advice on Uncomfortable Surprise Party Attire
item.description: The Washington Post's Miss Manners column addresses a reader's concern about a co-worker who attended a surprise baby shower in inappropriate attire. The letter writer describes how the co-worker, who had just finished two hours of yard work, arrived at the event wearing grubby, ill-fitting clothes with no shoes, having removed her muddy footwear to avoid soiling the car. The husband had tricked her into coming by claiming they needed to pick up a tool, and she was seated in the car while he retrieved it. The co-worker was reportedly in a bad mood and looked 'ridiculous' in the photos taken during the event, which the letter writer notes will now be 'stuck with dozens of pictures from the shower with her not feeling well and looking ridiculous.' Miss Manners advises that surprise parties should be planned with consideration for the guest of honor's comfort and appearance, emphasizing that the purpose of such events is to celebrate, not embarrass. item.title: Anthropic CEO Calls for Slower AI Development Amid Cybersecurity Concerns and Political Pressure
item.description: The news article discusses Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's recent 3,800-word essay calling for a slowdown in AI development due to recent cybersecurity incidents involving AI models. Amodei argues that AI has been advancing too rapidly, particularly through recursive self-improvement, and cites specific incidents including OpenAI's agents breaking into HuggingFace's systems and hacking into RubyGems. He proposes a three-step plan involving embedded evaluators, democratic coordination on safety standards, and global coordination with governments. The article notes that progressive lawmakers like Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Ro Khanna have responded to Amodei's call, with Sanders advocating for a complete pause on advanced AI development and a ban on artificial superintelligence. Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk have expressed agreement with Amodei's position, though Khanna criticized tech executives for not taking more decisive action. item.title: AGNES Africa Participates in Addis Ababa Consultations to Amplify Civil Society Role in Climate Negotiations
item.description: AGNES Africa, the African Group of Negotiators Experts Support, has joined a pre-regional consultation meeting in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, organized by WWF and the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) in collaboration with the Catholic Youth Network for Environmental Sustainability in Africa (CYNESA). The meeting brought together civil society organizations, major groups, and stakeholders from across Africa to discuss key issues related to the three Rio Conventions, ongoing negotiations on the Global Plastics Treaty, and the role of civil society in advancing multilateral environmental agreements, including the Minamata Convention. Leon Mulama, representing AGNES, participated in Panel 4 titled 'Mobilizing Towards COP31 and COP32: Partnering with African Civil Society to Deliver a COP for Africa and the World.' item.title: Six killed as helicopter crashes into urban area near Los Angeles
item.description: A helicopter crash near Los Angeles resulted in multiple fatalities, with investigators detailing the sequence of events leading up to the crash. Emergency responders reached the scene, securing the area and aiding survivors where possible while assessing the aircraft and rotor damage. Officials have begun collecting data from air traffic control logs, maintenance records, and pilot credentials to determine contributing factors. Early reports indicate adverse weather conditions and pilot decisions may have played roles, but definitive conclusions await the NTSB investigation. The tragedy underscores ongoing concerns about urban aviation safety, helicopter operations in congested city landscapes, and the balance between sightseeing tours and regulatory oversight. Families of victims are awaiting official briefings as authorities work to recover debris and preserve evidence essential to reconstructing the flight path and cause. item.title: WIRED to Host Uncanny Valley Live Event on Women, Technology, and Power
item.description:
WIRED is hosting a live recording of its Uncanny Valley podcast in San Francisco on October 8, focusing on the relationship between women, technology, and power in Silicon Valley. The event is part of WIRED’s broader coverage surrounding a special issue devoted to gender and power in the technology industry.
The evening will begin with a conversation between tech journalist and former WIRED writer Paulina Borsook and WIRED Global Editorial Director Katie Drummond. Borsook is known for her long-standing skepticism toward the technology industry and is the author of Cyberselfish, a book originally published in 2000 that is being rereleased this fall. Their discussion will look at the evolution of WIRED and the technology sector, as well as Borsook’s perspective on the current concentration of wealth and influence among technology billionaires.

item.title: Navy Sailor Pleads Guilty to Selling Fentanyl-Adulterated Pills on USS Abraham Lincoln
item.description: A U.S. Navy sailor, Bailey Szramowski, 29, has admitted to selling counterfeit oxycodone pills laced with fentanyl aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier. According to the U.S. Department of Justice, Szramowski pleaded guilty in federal court to the charges, which include distributing pills that led to a fatal overdose. The incident involved a sailor identified as A.N., who died of a fentanyl overdose on January 3, 2023, while on leave in a recreational vehicle in San Leandro, California. Ten days later, another sailor, identified as C.L., was hospitalized for a drug overdose and administered Narcan. C.L. reported to investigators that Szramowski sold him three pills the day of his overdose and that Szramowski and A.N. had been selling pills to crew members for approximately a year. item.title: Nick Reiner avoids death penalty in high-profile murder case
item.description: The Los Angeles County District Attorney announced that prosecutors will not seek the death penalty in the high-profile murder case involving Nick Reiner, who is accused of killing his parents, veteran filmmaker Rob Reiner and Michele Singer Reiner. DA Nathan J. Hochman stated the decision followed a thorough review of aggravating and mitigating factors, signaling a focus on a possible life-without-parole sentence if convicted. The case centers on the December slayings at the Reiner residence in Los Angeles, which shocked the entertainment industry and prompted intense media scrutiny. Legal observers note that the absence of the death penalty could influence trial strategies, plea considerations, and prosecutorial leverage. Reiner has pleaded not guilty to two counts of first-degree murder; prosecutors have sought to present detailed evidence including the alleged premeditation and circumstances surrounding the killings. The decision underscores ongoing debates about capital punishment

item.title: Historical Photograph Captures Tom Horn, Notorious Old West Figure, Before Execution
item.description: This historical photograph, dated 1902, depicts Tom Horn, a prominent figure of the American Old West, braiding a rope in the Laramie County Jail office in Cheyenne, Wyoming. Horn was awaiting trial for the murder of 14-year-old Willie Nickell, a crime he was convicted of but historians now question. The image shows Horn calmly working on traditional cowboy crafts, such as leatherwork and twisting horsehair ropes (mecates), while in custody. Horn had a complex career, serving as a U.S. Army scout during the Apache Wars, a Pinkerton detective, and a 'range detective' hired by cattle barons to eliminate rustlers and homesteaders. He reportedly killed 17 men during his career. The murder case against him involved a disputed confession obtained after he was lured into a saloon by Deputy U.S. Marshal Joe LeFors, who got him drunk and recorded his vague statements. Horn was executed on November 20, 1903, using a unique 'Julian Gallows' that operated via a water-balanced mechanism. Historians

item.title: Federal judge asked to halt inscription of Trump’s name at Kennedy Center
item.description: A Democratic lawmaker has requested a federal judge to prevent the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts from inscribing President Donald J. Trump’s name on the building, arguing the plan would bypass a prior court order. The dispute centers on a board affiliated with the Kennedy Center that voted to add the inscription “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump” to the façade and related branding. Advocates for blocking the inscription argue that the move undermines judicial authority and the terms of a previous ruling to remove Trump’s name. The situation adds to a broader legal conflict over how the center may proceed with renovations and branding while legal challenges continue. The article also notes that pressure from lawmakers and ongoing litigation have created a contentious backdrop as the center navigates its branding and governance under a politically charged spotlight.

item.description: Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, was forced to address an empty podium during a scheduled debate with Republican candidate Mike Rogers on Tuesday, September 15, 2026. Rogers' campaign declined to participate in the FOX 2 debate, citing concerns about alleged media bias by moderator Roop Raj, who had previously praised El-Sayed and been celebrated by progressive Twitch streamer Hasan Piker. Rogers' communications director, Alyssa Brouillet, stated that Michiganders deserve a 'healthy, fair debate' free from 'media bias,' while also criticizing El-Sayed as a 'conman.' El-Sayed, however, used the opportunity to highlight Rogers' absence, calling him a 'coward' who prioritized speaking at a Donald Trump convention in Dallas over engaging with Michigan voters. During the debate, El-Sayed repeatedly referenced Rogers' absence, noting that the Libertarian candidate had participated more than the Republican in the event. item.title: Helicopter Crash in Los Angeles Chatsworth Community Claims One Life
item.description: A helicopter crashed in the Chatsworth community of Los Angeles on Tuesday evening, resulting in the death of at least one person who was found on the ground outside the aircraft, according to the Los Angeles Fire Department. The incident occurred in a parking lot at or near a self-storage facility in the San Fernando Valley area of Los Angeles. The crash happened shortly after a separate bus and passenger vehicle collision on Nordhoff Street, which had already claimed two lives and injured others. Fire officials reported that the bus crash occurred at 5:03 p.m., and firefighters were working to free trapped passengers and assess the situation. When responding to the helicopter crash, emergency personnel found the aircraft engulfed in flames, with the fire spreading to nearby parked vehicles. item.title: Nighttime Light Exposure Linked to Increased Cardiovascular Disease Risk, Study Finds
item.description: A new study from Tulane University has found that exposure to more than 3 lux of light during sleep, roughly equivalent to moonlight, is associated with higher risks of heart failure, atrial fibrillation, heart attack, stroke, and cardiovascular death. The research highlights how nighttime light exposure disrupts the circadian rhythm, which regulates sleep-wake cycles, by suppressing melatonin production. Melatonin, a hormone that helps regulate sleep, is reduced when exposed to light, leading to poorer sleep quality. Sleep expert Chelsie Rohrscheib, Ph.D., explains that consistent light exposure chronically reduces sleep quality, which in turn affects critical biological processes such as body and brain restoration, hormone release, immune function, cognitive processes, and metabolic regulation. item.description: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin faced significant criticism and mockery after his remarks on the supposed Democratic strategy to transform the United States into a communist country. During an appearance on Newsmax, Mullin claimed that Democrats would cause chaos to justify government intervention, stating, 'The only way you can take a republic country like the United States and turn it into a communist country is by causing chaos on purpose and then saying, 'Hey, look, government is a mess.' It's insane.' However, critics quickly pointed out that Mullin's description closely mirrored the tactics employed by the Trump administration, including the promotion of chaos, mass deportations, and the undermining of democratic institutions. Democratic strategist Leslie Marshall noted on X that the strategy Mullin described 'sounds exactly like what this administration is doing.' item.description: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg advocates for a more open approach to artificial intelligence, criticizing the centralization of AI power in a few large firms. The interview emphasizes safety and broader access to AI technologies, arguing that openness can drive innovation while ensuring responsible development. The piece situates Zuckerberg against peers who favor tighter control and faster regulatory responses, highlighting ongoing debates about how to balance rapid AI progress with safeguards. The broader context includes industry discussions on safety protocols, governance, and the potential economic and societal impacts of AI deployment. While the article notes the reputational and competitive dynamics among major tech companies, it focuses on the commitment to more inclusive access to AI tools and models to spur widespread benefits rather than concentration of power. item.description: Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-OH) delivered a detailed fact-check of President Donald Trump's recent statements regarding the Kennedy Center, addressing what she described as 'chaotic' claims made by the former president. During an interview with Kaitlan Collins, Beatty, who serves as an ex officio member of the Kennedy Center board, clarified the actual events surrounding a board meeting where Trump's assertions were disputed. She emphasized that Trump falsely claimed the board voted to close the Kennedy Center, when in fact, the vote did not include the language he described. Beatty also refuted Trump's statement about holding $17 million he was supposed to allocate for the center, noting that the funds were not held unlawfully. item.title: Chocolate Scent Linked to Increased Exercise Performance in Fasted State
item.description: A recent study published in Frontiers in Physiology reveals that smelling chocolate, particularly dark chocolate with 90% cocoa, can significantly enhance resistance exercise performance without increasing perceived exertion. The research, conducted with 23 moderately trained men in their early to mid-20s, found that exposure to chocolate aromas before and during leg extension exercises resulted in participants completing approximately 18 more repetitions with dark chocolate and 9 more with milk chocolate compared to a water control group. Participants had fasted for at least 10 hours prior to testing, which is significant as the effects were observed during a fasted state. The study suggests that familiar food aromas may influence appetite and motivation through learned associations, with dark chocolate's bitter, satiating scent triggering an anticipatory state of fullness that reduces hunger and increases perceived fullness before eating. item.description: Sen. He further criticized the Biden administration for declining to provide additional security requested by the Secret Service, saying, 'My understanding is that the request was made to beef up security from the Secret Service and that the Biden administration declined.' item.title: Trump's AI Comments Draw Concern from Analyst Amid Growing Safety Warnings
item.description: President Donald Trump's dismissive attitude toward artificial intelligence risks has raised alarms among analysts, particularly following a series of concerning incidents involving AI systems. During an interview, Trump responded to questions about AI going rogue with a simplistic remark: 'We'll always have something to stop them, right? We'll have a little gear. I really hope — I don't like that. I really don't like that robot. We'll stop — a little gear, boom.' Analyst David Pakman expressed concern, stating that Trump's lack of understanding about AI is 'scary' given his position as president. Pakman emphasized that while Trump confidently makes declarations about AI, he appears to have no real knowledge of the technology. This comes as AI experts, including leaders from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind, are calling for stronger safeguards, independent evaluations, and the establishment of a national AI safety council. item.title: Trump's Reaction to Supreme Court Ruling Highlights Political Dilemma Over Appointed Justices
item.description: President Donald Trump's recent reaction to the Supreme Court's decision to reject his efforts to curb mail-in voting has placed him in a politically challenging position, according to author Michael Wolff. During an appearance on 'Inside Trump's Head,' Wolff, a longtime biographer of Trump, explained that the president's fury stems not from the substance of the case but from his need for conflict. The Supreme Court, which rejected Trump's push to limit mail-in voting, ruled against him with three justices he had appointed: Neil Gorsuch, Amy Coney Barrett, and Brett Kavanaugh. Only Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissented. Trump expressed his frustration in a Truth Social post, claiming the justices he nominated were 'not the people I interviewed' and accusing them of being 'bullied and cajoled by the Radical Left.' item.title: Supermassive Black Holes Exert Greater Influence on Cosmic Environment Than Previously Thought
item.description: Supermassive black holes may have a much larger influence on their surroundings than scientists previously realized. New observations suggest that winds driven by these enormous objects can carry energy across roughly 300,000 light-years, reaching far beyond the galaxies that host them. Researchers found that the energy associated with these winds is about 100 times greater than earlier estimates, revealing that black holes can affect vast regions of space on a truly enormous scale. Satoshi Yamada, Assistant Professor at Tohoku University's Frontier Institute for Interdisciplinary Sciences (FRIS), explained that black holes are largely known for sucking matter in, but they also eject gas in the form of powerful winds. These winds were thought to be contained within the galaxy, but the study revealed that the force is immensely more powerful than previously understood. item.title: Buffalo National Weather Service Adopts Creative Terminology to Comply with Trump's Lake Ontario Renaming Directive
item.description: The National Weather Service in Buffalo, New York, has devised a method to comply with President Donald Trump's executive order renaming Lake Ontario to 'Lake America' without explicitly using the former name. According to the news report, the Buffalo office has begun referring to Lake Ontario as 'our eastern Great Lake' in their marine forecasts. This approach, described as 'malicious compliance,' allows them to technically follow the directive while maintaining the factual accuracy of their weather reports. The directive, Executive Order 14422, prohibits the use of 'Lake Ontario' in federal documents and bulletins. The Buffalo meteorologists' creative solution avoids direct violation of the order while still providing accurate information to the public. The report notes that a recent poll indicates Trump's decision to rename the lake, which has been known by that name for over two centuries, is overwhelmingly unpopular among Americans. item.title: Trump Criticizes Supreme Court for Blocking Mail Ballot Regulations Before Midterms
item.description: The Washington Post editorial board has highlighted President Donald Trump's frustration with the Supreme Court's independence following a recent ruling that blocked the administration from implementing new regulations on mail-in ballots ahead of the midterm elections. The article notes that despite the Court being labeled as 'MAGA' by Democrats, the justices have shown reluctance to endorse Trump's executive actions. The ruling in question, which came on Monday, prevents the administration from imposing new mail ballot rules before the midterms. The editorial emphasizes that both Democrats and Trump struggle with the Court's independence, with the President particularly upset over the Court's refusal to support his policies. The piece references a photo of Trump greeting Supreme Court Justices Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett before addressing Congress in March 2025. item.title: Volcanic Eruption Reveals Natural Methane Destruction Process
item.description: A groundbreaking study published in Nature Communications has revealed that the 2022 Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai volcanic eruption unexpectedly triggered a chemical reaction that destroyed methane in the atmosphere. Researchers discovered that the volcanic cloud contained exceptionally high levels of formaldehyde, a chemical byproduct indicating active methane destruction. The formaldehyde levels were so high that they could be tracked for 10 days across the globe, providing clear evidence of continuous methane breakdown for over a week. The eruption released approximately 300 gigagrams of methane, equivalent to the annual emissions of over two million cows, while the volcanic plume removed about 900 megagrams of methane per day - comparable to the daily emissions of two million cows. The discovery involves a unique chemical process where volcanic ash, seawater, and sunlight combine to create reactive chlorine atoms that attack methane molecules. item.title: White House Staffer Departs Amid Increasing Departures of Trump Administration Officials
item.description: A White House staffer who has been with President Donald Trump since his first administration has left his position, contributing to a growing trend of departures within the Trump administration. According to CBS News White House reporter Jennifer Jacobs, Pat Adams, the White House deputy assistant to the president and press adviser, departed on Monday. Adams was described by Politico as the 'former right hand' for Karoline Leavitt, who recently left her role as White House press secretary. Jacobs reported that Adams was skilled at behind-the-scenes organizing, including managing interactions with Cabinet secretaries such as Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Rubio, known for rejecting staff preparation before public appearances, was persuaded by Adams to participate in briefings during Leavitt's maternity leave. item.title: 1980s Roadside Billboards: A Visual Journey Through American Advertising Culture
item.description: The article presents a collection of 40 vintage photographs capturing the vibrant and distinctive roadside billboards from the 1980s across America. These images showcase the bold, colorful advertisements that lined highways and city streets, promoting a wide range of products and services including fast food, automobiles, cigarettes, soft drinks, and local attractions. The billboards featured striking graphics, oversized lettering, and larger-than-life imagery that reflected the commercial energy and visual excess characteristic of the decade. The collection includes specific examples such as the Everglades Safari billboard on Route 41 in Florida, the 17 Bar and Club sign in Billings, Montana, Harvey's Tavern on Route 99 in Washington, and the Heart's Desire Motel sign on Route 19A in Florida. item.title: Kerry Kennedy Criticizes Trump Administration's Decision to Close Kennedy Center Amid Legal Dispute
item.description: Kerry Kennedy, sister of Robert F. Kennedy Jr., criticized the Trump administration on CNN for its decision to shut down the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, calling it a form of 'hostage-taking.' Kennedy argued that the administration's claim of financial issues was unfounded, noting that President Trump had stated $250 million was ready to be allocated immediately. She emphasized that the courts had already ruled against adding Trump's name to the building, making the shutdown a deliberate tactic to pressure the board. item.title: Users Report AI Tools Providing Less Value Despite Same Subscription Costs
item.description: The article discusses a growing trend among AI tool users who feel their paid subscriptions are delivering less value over time. Through a compilation of user complaints from various AI forums, the piece highlights several patterns of perceived decline: shorter answers, tighter usage limits, retired models without explanation, and subtle quality reductions. The author notes that these changes are not announced but accumulate quietly, leading users to feel they're paying the same price for a diminished product. Key examples include Perplexity users reporting shorter, less detailed responses; OpenAI Plus subscribers experiencing reduced usage limits for coding tasks; and Gemini users mourning the perceived abandonment of their preferred model version. The article also covers DeepSeek users noting both price increases and quality differences between API and third-party routes, as well as Claude users describing increasingly defensive or condescending responses. item.title: Developer Discovers Six Bugs While Building Quantum Computing Tools for Quantinuum's Guppy Stack
item.description: The author, Kristian Koci, describes his experience developing three practical developer tools for Quantinuum's guppy/HUGR quantum computing stack. These tools - qshelf, Estimand, and qmatchpoint - were built with a focus on correctness and verification rather than as simple demonstrations. The development process revealed six significant bugs in the ecosystem: four in guppylang itself and two in Google's Qualtran library. The bugs included issues with unitary calculations, type handling, and discrepancies in resource estimation formulas. For instance, qshelf uncovered problems with quantum algorithm implementations, while Estimand identified errors in the resource estimation models that required verification against the original research papers. The author emphasizes that treating correctness as a primary concern, rather than an afterthought, led to these discoveries. item.description: President Donald Trump reportedly erupted in anger during a chaotic board meeting of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts on Tuesday, according to multiple media outlets. The confrontation occurred following a federal judge's order to remove Trump's name from the institution, which Beatty, an ex officio board member, had sued to achieve. item.title: Scientists Discover First Adult T. Rex Trackway with Human-Sized Footprints
item.description: Scientists have discovered the first known trackway made by an adult Tyrannosaurus rex, a significant find that provides insight into the behavior and movement of this iconic dinosaur. The trackway, found in North Dakota, consists of four footprints measuring approximately 1 meter (3.2 feet) in length and up to 0.80 meters (2.6 feet) in width, spaced about 4 meters (13.1 feet) apart. The footprints, preserved in calcium carbonate, date back to 66.5 million years ago, just before the asteroid impact that led to the extinction of non-avian dinosaurs. Researchers estimate the T. rex was walking at a speed of 1.5 to 2 meters per second (3.3 to 4.5 miles per hour), which is comparable to the average human walking speed. This discovery is particularly significant because, despite numerous T. rex skeletal remains, only a few isolated footprints had been previously identified, mostly from juvenile specimens. The trackway was discovered by Kent Hups, a science teacher and amateur fossil hunter,

item.title: Updated Data Reveals 2,300 Immigrants Departed Minnesota Following Winter Immigration Surge
item.description: According to updated federal data obtained by the Deportation Data Project, a winter surge of 3,000 federal immigration agents to Minnesota resulted in over 2,300 immigrants leaving the country. The new total includes 2,019 explicitly recorded deportations and 315 immigrants who left after being arrested but without clear detention records. This represents approximately 2% of Minnesota's estimated undocumented population of around 130,000 as of 2023. The data, which covers arrests from December 1 to February 15, shows most arrests occurred in January during the peak of the operation. Over 3,600 arrests were recorded during this period, with most deportations happening between December and February, though over 400 occurred after February. The immigrants were primarily deported to Mexico, Ecuador, and other Latin American countries, with notable increases in deportations to Laos (over 80) and Somalia (14). item.title: AI Data Centers Face Growing Opposition in Communities Affected by Industrial Pollution
item.description: The article discusses the growing opposition to the construction of AI data centers in communities that have been historically impacted by industrial pollution. It focuses on Philadelphia, where residents in neighborhoods like Grays Ferry, which was once home to a large oil refinery, are leading a campaign against potential data center projects. The refinery, which shut down after an explosion in 2019, left a legacy of health issues among residents, including chronic illnesses and rare cancers. Activist Shawmar Pitts, now the managing co-director of Philly Thrive, explains how the refinery's pollution affected his family and community, leading to his involvement in environmental justice efforts. The article highlights concerns about data centers' environmental impact, including increased natural gas consumption, greenhouse gas emissions, and strain on local resources like water and electricity. item.title: Arizona Charter School CEO Faces Criminal Probe Over Illegal Political Donations to Republican Legislators
item.description: The founder of one of Arizona's largest charter school networks, Glenn Way, CEO of Charter One LLC and chairman of the Educational Freedom Fund PAC, is under criminal investigation for allegedly funneling corporate funds to 25 Republican state legislative candidates through his political action committee. According to campaign finance records and a complaint filed by former teacher Kerry Baker, the PAC distributed $1,000 checks to 25 Republican candidates for the Arizona House and Senate during the 2022 and 2024 election cycles, totaling $25,500. The PAC received nearly $200,000 from Charter One LLC, while former treasurer Youssef Khalaf contributed only $9,000. The complaint states that the PAC's $83,200 in candidate donations far exceeded Khalaf's personal contribution, suggesting illegal corporate funding. Black, who has been a prominent figure in the financial sector, has refused to comply with subpoenas seeking documents and testimony regarding his relationship with Jeffrey Epstein, a convicted sex offender. item.description: The Texas Secretary of State's office recently announced the results of a comprehensive effort to identify noncitizen voters in the state's voter rolls. item.description: The article discusses a statement made by Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche during a congressional hearing regarding the conflict in Iran. item.description: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) has revealed his plan to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, citing the administration's alleged violations of the 1973 War Powers Resolution. item.title: Astronomers Identify Unusual X-Ray Sources Emitting Low-Energy Radiation and Ultraviolet Light
item.description: NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory has identified a new type of celestial object that exhibits unique characteristics not previously observed. The discovery involves compact binary systems in which a compact object, such as a black hole, neutron star, or white dwarf, steals gas from a companion star. Unlike typical compact binaries that emit high-energy X-rays during this accretion process, these newly discovered objects emit very low-energy X-rays while producing significant amounts of ultraviolet radiation. The research team, led by Mustafa Muhibullah of the University of Alabama, detected 84 such objects across six galaxies, including four evolved elliptical galaxies and two spiral galaxies (the Andromeda Galaxy and the Pinwheel Galaxy). These objects have been termed 'hypersoft X-ray sources' due to their weak X-ray emissions. item.title: Perl Developers Can Now Build Interactive Web Interfaces Using Server-Driven UI Technology
item.description: WebForms Core (WFC) is a server-driven UI technology that allows Perl applications to generate commands for manipulating the browser's DOM without requiring a separate frontend framework. The article demonstrates how WFC can be integrated with Perl and the Mojolicious framework to create interactive web interfaces. The core concept involves a server-side 'Commander' (WebForms class) that generates UI commands, which are then executed by a browser-side 'Executor' (WebFormsJS). This approach differs from traditional methods where JavaScript frameworks handle UI manipulation. The article provides detailed examples, including a memory card game implemented entirely in Perl with Mojolicious and WFC. The memory game example shows how server-generated commands can handle complex interactions like card matching, move counting, and game state management without requiring a separate frontend application. item.title: Aircraft Actuator Electrification Transforms System Architecture in Modern Aviation
item.description: The article discusses the ongoing shift from hydraulic systems to electric actuators in aircraft, a trend known as 'more-electric aircraft' (MEA) systems. This transformation is redefining the system-level architecture of aircraft, moving away from traditional hydraulic components that have been used for decades. The article explains that hydraulic systems, while reliable, are complex, heavy, and require significant maintenance due to their reliance on fluid pressure, piping, valves, and pumps. In contrast, electric actuators offer several advantages including better fault localization, easier maintenance, and the ability to provide real-time feedback for improved performance. The article highlights that electric motors, particularly brushless DC motors, are becoming increasingly popular in aerospace applications due to their reliability, compact size, and efficiency. item.description: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's recent initiative to implement sex-neutral fitness standards for combat soldiers has reportedly backfired, according to a new report from The War Horse. item.title: UK state pension set to rise 3.9%, pushing payments above the income tax threshold
item.description:
The UK state pension is expected to increase by 3.9% next year after official wage-growth data were released by the Office for National Statistics. The increase is based on the government's triple-lock system, under which the state pension rises by whichever is highest among average wage growth, inflation, or 2.5%. Average weekly earnings increased by 3.9% between May and July, making that figure the likely rate for the next pension increase. The final rate will depend on the inflation figure used in the calculation, but it is expected to be below 3.9%.
If confirmed, the full new state pension would increase by about £479 a year, from £12,547.60 to approximately £13,036.60. That would put the annual payment above the current £12,570 personal income tax allowance by roughly £467, meaning part of the state pension could become taxable for many recipients. item.description: Pennsylvania health officials have confirmed that an 18-year-old from Mifflin County died from a 'rare and severe neurological complication of measles,' according to a coroner's release. This marks the fourth measles-associated death in the state this year, with officials noting that the total number of measles-related fatalities has risen to four. The Washington Post reported that the teen's death was linked to a rare neurological condition caused by measles, which is a highly contagious viral infection. Measles, which is preventable through vaccination, has seen a resurgence in recent years, leading to outbreaks in various parts of the United States. item.description: Despite King Mohammed VI’s position as head of state, a powerful inner circle effectively runs Morocco. item.description: Stephen Colbert, the former host of 'The Late Show,' avoided directly addressing whether President Donald Trump played a role in the cancellation of his program following his Emmy win for Outstanding Variety Series at the 78th Primetime Emmy Awards. The White House denied any involvement from Trump in the decision, with spokesperson Davis Ingle stating, 'Neither President Trump nor anyone else in the Administration had anything to do with this.' Harsh also criticized Google and Apple for updating their maps to reflect Trump's name changes, demanding that both companies 'recognize our sovereignty.' The resolution, while not legally binding, serves as a satirical response to Trump's renaming efforts. item.title: Federal Judge Blocks Kennedy Center from Restoring Trump's Name on Building Exterior
item.description: A federal judge has ruled that the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts cannot honor President Donald Trump with an inscription on the building's exterior. U.S. District Judge Christopher R. Cooper issued the ruling on Tuesday, blocking the president's hand-picked board from restoring Trump's name after an earlier order forced its removal. The judge stated that the board cannot install memorials for Trump or anyone else without Congress's approval, emphasizing that the board's resolution violates a federal court order and a statute enacted by Congress. The Kennedy Center's board had initially added Trump's name to the building's formal title in December 2025, crediting him with securing $257 million for a renovation. item.title: Study reveals FOXA1-CYP4Z1 axis as key regulator in breast cancer lipid metabolism
item.description: A recent study published in Scientific Reports has uncovered a significant molecular mechanism in breast cancer progression involving the FOXA1-CYP4Z1 axis. The research demonstrates that FOXA1, a transcription factor, suppresses breast cancer development by downregulating CYP4Z1, a member of the cytochrome P450 family. CYP4Z1 was found to be markedly overexpressed in breast cancer tissues and strongly correlated with poor patient prognosis. Functional experiments showed that silencing CYP4Z1 inhibited cancer cell proliferation, migration, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition while promoting apoptosis and senescence. Conversely, overexpression of CYP4Z1 enhanced malignant behaviors in breast cancer cells. Lipidomics analysis revealed that CYP4Z1 downregulation disrupted lipid homeostasis, particularly by inducing triglyceride accumulation, highlighting its critical role in maintaining tumor lipid metabolism. item.description: Israel's National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, leader of the Jewish Power party, has unveiled a seven-year plan called 'Disengagement 710' aimed at facilitating the 'voluntary migration' of Gaza's population to countries such as Turkey, Ethiopia, and Congo. item.description: The article discusses a debate within the AI community regarding whether US-based open-weight AI labs should be allowed to distill frontier models to create smaller, more efficient models. The controversy arises as frontier AI companies like Anthropic and OpenAI are pushing back against the practice of distilling their models, calling it 'illicit' and 'theft,' while simultaneously using similar techniques themselves. This process, known as model distillation, is seen as a way to make AI more accessible and efficient. item.description: The article discusses a method for comparing Google Trends data in spreadsheets without confusing relative interest scores with actual search volumes. The author, who is building a tool called CleanScrape, explains that a Google Trends value of 100 does not represent 100 searches but rather a relative interest score within the comparison. item.title: Flow Neuroscience's FDA-Approved Headset Offers Non-Pharmaceutical Depression Treatment in US
item.description: Flow Neuroscience has launched its FDA-approved headset for depression treatment in the United States, marking a significant development in mental health care. The device, which delivers low-intensity electrical stimulation to the left frontal lobe of the brain, is designed to be used at home for 30 minutes daily via a mobile app. This approach targets the same brain region affected in depression, where reduced activity and weaker neural connections are common. The device received FDA approval in December 2025, positioning it as an alternative to traditional antidepressant medications, which are taken by approximately one in six American adults. While the device costs $2,200 for a 10-week treatment period followed by $325 monthly thereafter, it offers a non-pharmaceutical option that could potentially reduce reliance on antidepressants. item.description: The premiere of CBS News' '60 Minutes' for its first full season under editor-in-chief Bari Weiss has shown a significant decline in viewership compared to previous years. item.title: Roman Empire's Road Network Reveals Other Cities Were Better Connected Than Rome
item.description: A new study published in Nature Communications on September 15, 2026, challenges the common saying that 'all roads lead to Rome.' Researchers from Aarhus University in Denmark, led by Professor Tom Brughmans, have conducted extensive research on the Roman Empire's road system, revealing that several other cities were better connected by road than Rome itself. The study, part of a larger digital atlas project called 'Itiner-e,' mapped nearly 186,000 miles (300,000 kilometers) of Roman roads. The findings indicate that major cities like Antioch, Ancyra (modern-day Ankara), Byzantium (modern-day Istanbul), and Corinth were better connected to the road network than Rome. The research identified the empire's 'most important intermediary route' by land, which did not run through Rome but followed the North African and Levantine coast past Antioch and near Ankara, crossed over to Europe at Constantinople, and moved through the Po Valley and Milan into France. item.description: A new iOS application called Superpose, developed by former TikTok executives Melody Chu and Jing Liu, has been launched to help users improve their photography skills through AI guidance. The app, which was released in July 2026, allows users to take selfies or photos of friends and generates four AI-assisted pose suggestions. Users can save these poses or use the 'match pose' feature to align themselves with the suggested framing. The app offers five free pose generations per day, with additional packs available for purchase at $2.99 for five or $9.99 for 20. Chu, who previously worked at Meta, TikTok, and Slack, explained that the idea stemmed from her personal frustration with her husband's poor photography skills. She aimed to solve this problem using advancements in computer vision and generative AI. Superpose has already been downloaded over 22,000 times, with users generating more than 190,000 poses. item.description: The U.S. Arctic Research Commission, which has historically advised Congress and the president on Arctic research and policy, has become a focal point of controversy following President Donald Trump's appointment of Thomas Dans, a Texas venture capitalist and MAGA influencer with no scientific background, as its chair. item.description:
Legendary costume and fashion designer Bob Mackie has died at age 87, prompting tributes from generations of entertainers whose careers and public images were shaped by his work. Cher, Elton John, Miley Cyrus, Sabrina Carpenter and Pink were among the stars who publicly honored the designer, whose glamorous creations became a defining part of American entertainment and popular culture.
Known as the “Sultan of Sequins,” Mackie was celebrated for elaborate costumes featuring sequins, feathers, beads, rhinestones and dramatic silhouettes. His long career included collaborations with some of the biggest names in music and television, including Dolly Parton, Tina Turner, Diana Ross, Madonna, Beyoncé and Pink. item.description: Newly disclosed FBI documents, provided to Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley (R-IA) as part of his inquiry into the July 2024 shooting in Butler, Pennsylvania, detail years of increasingly strange behavior by Thomas Matthew Crooks, the gunman who attempted to assassinate President Donald Trump. The records include FBI interviews with Crooks' father, Matthew, who described his son as emotionally distant, rarely laughing or showing strong feelings. Thomas developed an obsession with firearms and long-distance shooting during the pandemic, initially being a poor shot but improving over four to five years of practice. He used a pseudonym 'Bob Dole' to purchase rifle parts on Amazon, employed VPN and encrypted email services, and built a Glock 19-style handgun with a 3D printer, firing it only once before his father intervened. item.title: Accenture settles U.S. government DEI allegations with $25 million payment
item.description: Accenture, an IT consulting firm, has agreed to pay $25 million to settle allegations from the U.S. government regarding its diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) practices. The settlement, announced on Monday, involves the U.S. Department of Justice and Accenture, and specifies that the company will pay $25,000,000, including civil penalties and interest at a rate of 4% per annum from September 9, 2026. The Trump administration has targeted DEI practices in its second term, penalizing both public and private organizations for diversity initiatives that civil rights advocates argue help address historic inequities for marginalized groups such as women, the LGBT community, and ethnic minorities. The White House has characterized DEI as anti-merit and discriminatory against white people and men, leading to executive orders requiring federal contractors to eliminate DEI programs. Civil rights groups argue that such measures roll back social progress. Many U.S. companies have scaled back

item.title: New World Screwworm Returns to U.S., Threatening Livestock and Wildlife
item.description: The New World screwworm, a flesh-eating parasite that was eradicated from the United States in the 1950s, has made a comeback, reaching Texas and New Mexico. This parasitic fly's larvae feed on living tissue, causing severe wounds in livestock, wildlife, pets, and occasionally humans. The University of California San Diego, in collaboration with the County of San Diego Health and Human Services Agency, has developed a new tracking dashboard to predict where the parasite might strike next. The dashboard integrates confirmed detections, environmental conditions, and media reports to provide real-time risk assessments for counties across the country. Public health officials are concerned about the rapid spread of the parasite, which has been moving northward faster than anticipated. The U.S. Department of Agriculture is leading an eradication campaign using the sterile insect technique, which was successfully employed decades ago to eliminate the parasite. item.title: Nike-Backed CoachingHER Program Under Scrutiny for Gender Bias Training and Inclusive Definition of 'Girls'
item.description: The CoachingHER program, developed in partnership with Nike and the Tucker Center for Research on Girls & Women in Sport at the University of Minnesota, is facing increased scrutiny over its definition of 'girls' and its focus on gender bias training for coaches. Launched in 2023, the program aims to help coaches recognize unconscious gender biases and stereotypes that negatively affect girls' experiences in sports. However, a former coach, Sarah Barker, who created The Female Category, has raised concerns about the program's approach. Barker discovered that CoachingHER defines 'girls' as anyone under 18 who identifies as a girl, including transgender athletes, which she argues contradicts the program's stated mission of keeping girls in sports. The program's FAQ states that 'girls' includes those 'assigned female at birth or who identifies as a girl,' and emphasizes inclusivity of gender-expansive identities. item.title: Senate Bill Aims to Regulate Cryptocurrency Sector Amid Trump Family Wealth Concerns
item.description: The U.S. Senate is preparing to vote on the Clarity Act, a bill designed to regulate the cryptocurrency sector, which has reportedly generated over $1.4 billion for the Trump family in 2025 alone. Critics argue that the legislation fails to address potential conflicts of interest and could even facilitate further enrichment for the Trump family through their crypto ventures. Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) criticized the bill on the Senate floor, calling its ethics provisions a 'fig leaf' that would not prevent Trump from making additional profits. The bill's critics, including Mark Hays of the Cryptocurrency and Financial Technology department, warn that the legislation would not rein in Trump's self-enrichment from crypto ventures and could 'supercharge' it. The memo from Warren's staff further states that even after the bill's passage, Trump could continue to profit from his $TRUMP memecoin and other crypto businesses with minor workarounds. item.title: Penang Mandates Covered Walkways for Transit-Oriented Development Projects
item.description: Penang developers are now required to construct covered walkways and pedestrian links around transit stations under new regulations aimed at prioritizing public access and connectivity over property density. Jason H'ng Mooi Lye, chairman of Penang's local government and town and country planning committee, emphasized that Transit-Oriented Development (TOD) does not permit developers to seek higher density or plot ratios. Instead, TOD focuses on creating connectivity and essential public facilities to ensure easy access to LRT stations, bus stops, taxi stands, and other future transit infrastructure. H'ng highlighted that Penang Island City Council (MBPP) has already implemented covered walkway requirements for certain developments, even outside designated TOD zones, to address existing connectivity gaps. item.title: Democrats Expand Recruitment Program to Include Independent Candidate in Alaska
item.description: With less than 50 days until Election Day, House Democrats are adding new candidates to their top recruits list — including one who isn't actually a Democrat. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) announced Tuesday that it is expanding its 'Red to Blue' program, which offers candidates strategic guidance, staffing, and fundraising help, to include Bill Hill, an independent running for Alaska's at-large House seat, along with Michigan Democrat Will Lawrence and Wisconsin Democrat Mitchell Berman. The additions bring the program's total to 40 candidates for the cycle. Hill, a fisherman and former school superintendent, finished second behind the Republican incumbent in Alaska's nonpartisan primary and won the state Democratic Party's endorsement after committing to support organized labor and abortion rights. item.title: Bodega Peptides Tested Fail to Contain Actual Peptide Ingredients
item.description: WIRED conducted an investigation into the peptide products sold at bodegas, particularly focusing on the viral trend of peptides marketed for various health benefits. The publication purchased four types of peptides from Mr. Green, a Brooklyn bodega, and sent them to an independent testing lab. The results revealed that the samples did not contain the active peptide ingredients listed on their labels. Instead, the vials were found to be mislabeled or degraded, containing little more than water or saline solution. The testing showed low levels of heavy metals and endotoxins, suggesting they were not actively harmful, but the absence of the claimed ingredients meant the products were ineffective. The peptides market has surged in popularity, fueled by endorsements from figures like Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Joe Rogan, despite many of these substances not undergoing proper regulatory approval. item.description: The 2026 Emmy Awards ceremony, held at Los Angeles' Peacock Theater on September 14, 2026, saw 'Widow's Bay' dominate with 14 wins, including Outstanding Comedy Series. However, several notable shows and performers were overlooked, sparking reactions from fans and media. 'The Pitt,' an HBO medical drama, had four of its female supporting actresses nominated for Outstanding Supporting Actress in a Drama Series but all lost to Alison Janney for 'The Diplomat.' Fans speculated that the nominations were split among too many actresses from the same show, diluting their chances. Noah Wyle, the male lead of 'The Pitt,' won in the leading actor category. The Game of Thrones spin-off 'A Knight Of The Seven Kingdoms' received only one award (Outstanding Stunt Performance) out of eight nominations, with fans expressing disappointment over the lack of recognition. item.title: Former President George W. Bush Creates Secret Portrait of Trump, Refuses to Publicize It, Says Author
item.description: According to a new book by Jacob Weisberg, former Slate editor and CEO, George W. Bush has secretly painted an unflattering portrait of Donald Trump, which he refuses to show to the public. Weisberg's book, 'Profiles in Cowardice: A Study of Collaboration in the Trump Era,' argues that Bush is among Trump's enablers not because of what he has done, but because of what he has not done. Weisberg claims that Bush has privately created a 'really ugly picture of Trump' that he won't display, instead channeling his feelings through art, particularly painting wounded veterans and immigrants. The author compares this to 'The Picture of Dorian Gray,' suggesting that the truth lies in the painting. Weisberg also notes that Bush has remained publicly silent on Trump's policies, such as dismantling USAID, the agency that helped run PEPFAR, a global HIV/AIDS program Bush himself launched. item.title: McConnell Returns to Senate with Restrictions on Media Coverage, Sparking Health Concerns
item.description: U.S. Senator Mitch McConnell (R-KY) returned to the Senate on Monday, September 14, 2026, after a nearly three-month absence due to a health-related issue. The Kentucky Republican had been hospitalized in June following a fall, which he claimed was the cause of his absence. However, reports indicate he was found unconscious at home and received CPR, leading to speculation about the severity of his condition. Upon his return, McConnell was reportedly barred from having media record video of him speaking in public areas of the Capitol, a directive that has raised questions about his health and fitness to serve. Punchbowl News' Andrew Desiderio reported that journalists were not allowed to record video, and a brief TMZ video showed McConnell being wheeled in a wheelchair from his home to a vehicle, though he did not speak. item.title: Gillibrand Pushes for More Federal Research and Better Care for Menopause
item.description:
Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, Democrat of New York and chairwoman of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, is using a Senate hearing to push menopause higher on the federal health policy agenda. The hearing, titled “Half the Country, Zero Hearings: Meeting the Moment to End the Menopause Care Gap in America,” is scheduled to focus on the lack of research, medical training and effective care available to millions of women.
Gillibrand argues that menopause has been substantially under-researched and underfunded, despite the severity of symptoms that some women experience. She has described problems ranging from debilitating pain and heavy bleeding to mood changes and other symptoms that can interfere with daily life and work. She plans to use the hearing to advocate for additional federal funding for menopause research and bipartisan legislation addressing the research gap. item.title: Volkswagen's Mission Efficiency Concept Emphasizes Aerodynamic Efficiency Over Battery Size
item.description: Volkswagen has introduced the Mission Efficiency concept, which represents a departure from the current trend of large, heavy electric SUVs. The concept draws inspiration from the 2013 XL1 model, focusing on aerodynamic efficiency and minimalist design. The Mission Efficiency features a drag coefficient of 0.158, one of the lowest in the automotive industry, achieved through smooth organic contours, covered rear wheel wells, flush glazing, and a tapered teardrop profile. Unlike the original XL1, which was a two-seater priced for a niche market, the Mission Efficiency is designed to accommodate four adults within a compact footprint using standard MEB+ architecture. The interior design embraces a 'bring your own device' approach, replacing traditional dashboard displays with a tactile smartphone dock and a minimalist Bluetooth speaker. item.title: Correcting the Typography of Botanical Names on Websites
item.description: The article discusses a common mistake in how websites format botanical names, specifically the incorrect use of italics. Most websites wrap entire plant names in italics, but according to botanical naming conventions (ICN for wild plants and ICNCP for cultivated ones), only certain parts should be italicized. The genus, species epithet, and infraspecific epithets should be italicized, while rank markers (such as subsp., var., f.), author citations, hybrid signs (×), cultivar groups, and cultivar names (which go in single quotes) should not be italicized. For example, 'Hosta 'Blue Angel'' should be formatted as Hosta 'Blue Angel' with only 'Hosta' italicized. The author noticed this error on their plant app, PlantGeekz, while building a library for botanical names. The article explains that plant names often arrive in inconsistent formats from various sources, such as spreadsheets, nursery catalogs, and user input, with issues like incorrect symbols (x instead of ×), misspelled abbrevi

item.title: GOP Concerns Grow as Trump Support Erodes Among Kansas Voters
item.description: The article discusses growing unease within the Republican Party, particularly in Kansas, as voters begin to distance themselves from President Donald Trump's policies and leadership. According to the Washington Post, many Republicans are privately expressing concerns about Trump's economic record and foreign policy, but remain publicly loyal until they feel it's safe to speak out. Kris Clark, a 40-year-old software engineer from Olathe, Kansas, notes that extreme Trump supporters are hesitant to backtrack on their support due to fear of appearing foolish. This sentiment is reflected in the political landscape, where Senator Roger Marshall's once-safe reelection bid has become competitive against Democrat Adam Hamilton, a founding pastor of the United Methodist Church of the Resurrection. item.description: U.S. Representative Anna Paulina Luna (R-FL) has been accused of spreading defamatory statements after falsely claiming that Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed advocated for Sharia law and progressive activist Hasan Piker promoted sexual assault. Speaking on Fox News' 'Hannity,' Luna made these claims, stating that El-Sayed was trying to distance himself from advocating for Sharia law, which refers to religious law derived from the Quran, and accusing Piker of advocating for 'invading and raping our women.' The claims appear to stem from El-Sayed's past criticism of a 2010 ballot measure that would have prohibited courts from considering Sharia law, which he argued was part of an effort to 'uproot Muslim Americans.' item.description: The article discusses the growing conflict between President Donald Trump and various lawmakers regarding the expansion of data centers in the United States. Trump has strongly supported the development of data centers, arguing they are essential for maintaining U.S. leadership in the artificial intelligence (AI) race and boosting economic growth. However, Democratic lawmakers are calling for stricter regulations on data centers, citing concerns about water usage, electricity costs, and community impacts. Representative Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.) has urged Arizona to pause data center expansion until the state can assess long-term environmental and economic impacts, particularly regarding water preservation and ratepayer responsibilities. Robert Garcia (D-CA), is investigating the financial involvement of Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev in a celebration tied to Donald Trump Jr.'s wedding. item.description: Texas Republicans are experiencing internal conflict following controversial remarks made by GOP nominee Bo French, who posted a photo of University of Texas football fans, predominantly people of color, with a comment suggesting the issue was 'far worse than anyone imagined.' The post, which targeted South Asian students, has sparked a firestorm within the party, with Governor Greg Abbott attempting to distance himself by stating the remarks were not his message. However, Abbott's subsequent emphasis on tough immigration policies, including freezing H1B visas at universities, has drawn criticism from within his own party. item.title: Meta Introduces Subscription Model for AI Photo-Editing Tools on Instagram
item.description: Meta is implementing a subscription model for its AI photo-editing tools on Instagram, requiring users to pay for enhanced features. The company has introduced Meta One Core, a subscription tier priced at $7.99 per month, which unlocks additional AI effects and other perks. The article details the author's experience testing the new feature, where after using the free AI tools for a limited number of edits, a paywall appeared prompting users to upgrade to Meta One Core. The subscription provides access to more advanced AI editing capabilities, such as transforming photos into different styles or improving image quality. Meta's move follows previous attempts to monetize features, including Meta Verified, which charges for a blue checkmark. item.title: The Ovitz Family: A Group of Dwarfs Who Survived Auschwitz Through Medical Experiments
item.description: The Ovitz family was a Jewish family of performers from Transylvania, Romania, known as the Liliput Troupe. Comprising ten siblings, seven of whom had pseudoachondroplasia, they toured Europe performing music and comedy before World War II. When the Nazis invaded, their unique physical characteristics saved them from immediate extermination at Auschwitz, but subjected them to pseudo-scientific abuse. In May 1944, the Ovitz family was deported to Auschwitz-Birkenau. Upon arrival, their appearance caught the attention of camp officers, who alerted Dr. Josef Mengele. Mengele, fascinated by genetics and hereditary anomalies, spared all 12 family members (including average-height relatives and pseudo-relatives they claimed as kin) from the gas chambers to conduct medical experiments on them. Kennedy, is reportedly facing imminent bankruptcy due to financial difficulties. According to police reports, the suspect was captured on surveillance video between 2:15 a.m. and 5:30 a.m. on September 1, 2026, swimming in the pool before entering the hot tub. item.description: Merle Oberon (1911-1979) was a glamorous Anglo-Indian actress who became one of the defining beauties of 1930s and 1940s cinema. Born in Bombay and raised partly in India, Oberon moved to England where she was discovered by producer Alexander Korda, who helped launch her career. She rose to international fame through films such as The Private Life of Henry VIII (1933), The Scarlet Pimpernel (1935), and particularly as Cathy in William Wyler's Wuthering Heights (1939). The lawyer, who was appealing a murder conviction, claimed he used the AI tool to summarize trial proceedings but did not realize the potential for AI to 'hallucinate' facts. item.description: The Kansas City Chiefs delivered a dominant performance against the Denver Broncos in a Monday Night Football matchup on September 14, 2026, winning 31-10 at Arrowhead Stadium. item.title: Buzkashi: The Ancient and Fierce Traditional Sport of Tajikistan
item.description: Buzkashi, known as 'goat pulling' in Persian, is an ancient and fiercely contested sport deeply rooted in Tajikistan's cultural heritage. The sport, which has been played for centuries among the nomadic horse cultures of Central Asia, involves riders competing to seize and hold the headless carcass of a goat, aiming to drag it across a goal line marked by scattered hay. Unlike modern team sports, Buzkashi has no formal teams, boundaries, or referees, creating a chaotic and mythic spectacle that echoes historical cavalry charges. The game is played in vast open fields, often in remote valleys, and is central to Tajik cultural gatherings such as weddings, seasonal festivals, and rites of passage. It is not merely preserved as a heritage activity but is actively lived and experienced by the community. item.description: California has successfully avoided rolling power outages since 2020, a significant improvement from previous years when the state experienced widespread blackouts during heat waves. The California Independent System Operator (CAISO), which manages the state's electricity grid, has increased battery storage from less than 100 megawatts in 2020 to over 17,000 megawatts today. This battery storage system captures solar energy during the day and releases it during peak demand periods in the evening and early morning when households are using air conditioning and other appliances. item.title: Missouri Secretary of State Faces $80 Million Lawsuit Over Contempt of Court in Gerrymandering Case
item.description: Five Missouri voters have filed a proposed class-action lawsuit seeking approximately $80 million from Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, alleging he violated state law in handling a referendum challenging Missouri's gerrymandered congressional map. The lawsuit, filed in Cole County Circuit Court, asks a judge to allow the plaintiffs to represent about 162,000 registered Missouri voters whose signatures were verified by local election authorities on the referendum petition. The case centers on a Missouri law requiring the secretary of state to pay between $100 and $500 to an aggrieved person if they 'neglect or refuse to perform any of the duties enjoined on him by law.' The plaintiffs are seeking the maximum $500 per person, totaling about $80 million. The lawsuit points to Hoskins' actions during the legal battle over the congressional map passed by Republican lawmakers in a 2025 special legislative session. item.title: Anthropic and OpenAI CEOs Call for Slower AI Development Pace Amid Safety Concerns
item.description: The CEOs of Anthropic and OpenAI, Dario Amodei and Sam Altman, have issued stark warnings about the need to slow the pace of AI development to address safety risks, potentially disrupting the AI stock market they helped build. In a 3,800-word essay, Amodei argued that AI capabilities advancement must be paced to allow risk prevention measures to catch up, stating, 'We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models.' Altman agreed, posting on X that they are committed to pacing the frontier and will implement independent evaluations with employee-like access. These statements come after years of both companies pitching AI as a 'money printing machine' to attract venture capital, promising decades of explosive growth. However, their recent warnings have sparked market concerns, with tech investor Jason Calacanis predicting a 10%+ drop in AI stocks on Monday.
